Furthermore, the problems with EU sovereign debt have not fully abated. The Standard & Poor’s rating agency has again reduced Ireland’s debt rating in early February, moving to A-minus from A and maintaining its negative stance because of the uncertainty over how much more capital injection will be necessary for the domestic banking sector. The agency has said that it should have a much clearer picture by April and a decision will then be taken about whether to remove the negative stance. European economic data is mixed, with December inflation for the (then) 16-Eurozone nations above target at an annualised 5.3%, a two-year high. This was bloated by energy prices, although core inflation was nonetheless 3.3%. Consumer confidence has been falling while manufacturers’ confidence is rising. The European Central Bank has left interest rates on hold in the belief that the recent inflation figures are a blip and that “inflationary pressures over the medium term should remain contained”. Large shorts raise a prospect of spiky rallies, but downside risk persists and is the stronger underlying shorter-term influence** Gold’s tumble in price during January came amidst both long liquidation and fresh short-side

selling. Of itself this is not surprising, but what is important is the fact that at the end of January, the outright short-side “investor” position on Comex was at its largest since early June 2005, and it is likely that short positions have also been implemented elsewhere. This means that we should be alert to the possibility of short-covering rallies in the next few weeks. It looks as if the escalating tension in the Middle East, which has no doubt contributed to the tightness in the physical gold market, has already precipitated one such rally, but gold actually made little upside headway, even though the dollar was under pressure. On this basis, and given the underlying fundamentals in the gold market, we continue to see the risk of further downward price pressure in the coming weeks, as important buying seasons draw to a close (the Chinese New Year fell on 3rd February and the Indian wedding season runs to 15th February). Obviously, though, the surrounding economic, fiscal and political environment has to be taken into account. If Middle Eastern tensions worsen (as we write there is an increasing possibility of demonstrations in Jordan, following the rйgime change in Tunisia and the shifting balance of power in Egypt), then gold is likely to remain in favour and our forecast test of the lower end of the $1,300-$1,400 range may not develop. If the situation is resolved as peacefully as possible, then there is still a risk of further gold weakness before prices stabilise in March and April in readiness for renewed strength later in the year. Indeed the tensions in the Middle East have heightened these longer-term inflationary risks, with oil now trading in excess of $100/bbl. ##### **A test of $1,600 towards year-end is still a disticnt possiblity** We continue to expect a fresh body of investment to develop in the second half of the year, taking prices towards a test of $1,600 by year-end. This is predicated primarily on increasing expectation of inflationary pressures in the western world and the extended period for which interest rates will be held down. That said, inflationary pressures are already a cause for concern in some emerging markets and certainly in China, where it has been a driver behind very strong Chinese investment demand for gold in recent months. Looking further, professional investment demand is expected to wane towards the end of 2012 as the dollar enjoys a secular recovery, although an improvement in jewellery demand should help to contain the decline in price. ##### **Recent trading; “professional” selling meets “grass roots” buying** |**~~Gold Supply-Demand & Pric~~**

Analysis of the trading and open interest figures suggests that the “industrial” users of the exchange reduced both their long and their short positions during January. This also points to uncertainty. Some trade buyers presumably locked in futures prices in fear of further falls; others took future cover in expectation of a price recovery. The hike in margins in the mid-month may also have contributed to some position reductions. ##### **Short side trading was more important in January than long liquidation** By the last Tuesday of January (the most recent available figure) the net non-commercial and non-reportable or “investor” position on Comex stood at 6,710 tonnes, a drop of 1,204 tonnes or 15% against the recent peak (endDecember) of 7,914 tonnes. The outright investor long fell by 829 tonnes during the month, but the short position increased by 1,204 tonnes.
